name: Olive-Ocher
lede: Olive-Ocher is a dark, muted yellow that pairs two of the oldest color words in the language: olive, the fruit, and ocher, the earth pigment.

sections.title: Fruit and earth together
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 color book places this value on plate XXX, hue 21″, and our library carries no later citation for it, so it was not picked up by the 1930 or 1955 dictionaries [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[light-cadmium]], [[bistre-green]] and [[tennis]], at 2.6, 2.7 and 2.8 ΔE [1]. The hyphen marks a deliberate blend of the two older words rather than a single new source [1].

The nearest library neighbor is Light Cadmium [1]. Compare [[khaki|Khaki]] and [[marigold|Marigold]], names our archive finds sharing its canvases most [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive of 23,781 paintings finds a color within six units of this one in 920, about 3.9 percent, as photographed [2]. It is strongly concentrated in Indian painting: 112 of 721 Indian works carry it, over four times the archive rate, and Kalighat works carry it in 41 of 96, eleven times the rate [2]. The earliest dated match is a 1230 crucifix panel, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. The match is a screen-color comparison on aged, varnished paintings, not a pigment test [2].
